title: TensorFlow and Keras Basics
summary: TensorFlow with Keras offers a high-level, beginner-friendly way to build neural networks with minimal code. While PyTorch dominates research, many production systems and tutorials use Keras, so knowing both frameworks makes you versatile and employa
content:
# TensorFlow and Keras Basics ##### Eleven lines versus ninety Two students at a hackathon in Bhopal were given the same task: classify Fashion-MNIST images, best accuracy in ninety minutes. One wrote PyTorch. Custom `Dataset`, `DataLoader`, `nn.Module`, a manual training loop with `zero_grad`/`backward`/`step`, a validation function, an early-stopping counter, checkpoint saving. Around ninety lines. He finished with twenty minutes to spare and got 0.912. The other wrote Keras: ```python model = keras.Sequential([ layers.Flatten(input_shape=(28, 28)), layers.Dense(256, activation="relu"), layers.Dropout(0.2), layers.Dense(10), ]) model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy"]) model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=15, validation_split=0.1) ``` Eleven lines. Done in fifteen minutes. He got 0.911, then spent the remaining seventy-five minutes trying architectures and finished at 0.923. Neither framework is better. They optimise for different things, and **knowing both makes you more employable** — PyTorch dominates research and most GenAI work, while a great deal of production tooling, enterprise codebases, and tutorial material is Keras. Today you learn the second one, and more usefully, you learn what each is good at. ##### Where Keras fits TensorFlow is Google's numerical computing framework (Abadi et al., 2016). Keras is the high-level API on top of it, and since TensorFlow 2.0 it is the *primary* way to use TensorFlow. Keras 3 additionally runs on JAX and PyTorch backends, so the API is increasingly framework-agnostic. The philosophical difference: | | PyTorch | Keras | |---|---|---| | Training loop | You write it | `model.fit()` | | Control | Total | Via callbacks and overrides | | Boilerplate | High | Very low | | Debugging | Plain Python, easy | More layers to look through | | Research prototyping | Excellent | Good | | Fast standard models | Good | Excellent | | Deployment | TorchServe, ONNX | TF Serving, TFLite, TF.js | | Ecosystem for GenAI | Dominant (HF, most LLMs) | Smaller | The honest summary: **Keras is faster when your problem is standard; PyTorch is better when it is not.** Since most GenAI work involves unusual training loops, PyTorch dominates there — but the Keras skills transfer, because the underlying concepts are identical. ##### The Sequential API For a straight stack of layers, `Sequential` is the shortest path. ```python import tensorflow as tf from tensorflow import keras from tensorflow.keras import layers keras.utils.set_random_seed(42) (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data() x_train = x_train.astype("float32") / 255.0 # scale to [0, 1] x_test = x_test.astype("float32") / 255.0 class_names = ["T-shirt", "Trouser", "Pullover", "Dress", "Coat", "Sandal", "Shirt", "Sneaker", "Bag", "Ankle boot"] model = keras.Sequential([ keras.Input(shape=(28, 28)), layers.Flatten(), layers.Dense(256, activation="relu"), layers.BatchNormalization(), layers.Dropout(0.3), layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), layers.Dropout(0.2), layers.Dense(10), # raw logits ], name="fashion_mlp") model.summary() ``` `model.summary()` prints a table of layers, output shapes, and parameter counts. It is genuinely useful — check that the output shapes are what you expect and that your parameter count is sane. A model with 40 million parameters for Fashion-MNIST is a sign something is wrong. **Use `keras.Input(shape=...)` as the first entry** rather than passing `input_shape` to the first layer. It builds the model immediately, so `summary()` works before training. ##### Compiling `compile()` attaches the three things training needs: an optimiser, a loss, and metrics. ```python model.compile( optimizer=keras.optimizers.AdamW(learning_rate=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4), loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy", keras.metrics.SparseTopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3, name="top3")], ) ``` **The `from_logits=True` detail matters enormously.** Because the last `Dense` layer has no `softmax` activation, its output is raw logits, and the loss must know to apply log-softmax itself. Getting this wrong is the most common Keras bug: if you use `softmax` on the output layer *and* `from_logits=True`, softmax is applied twice and training degrades badly. Pick one convention — raw logits plus `from_logits=True` is numerically more stable and is what to prefer. **Loss selection:** | Labels look like | Loss | |---|---| | Integers `[3, 7, 1]` | `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy` | | One-hot `[[0,0,0,1,...]]` | `CategoricalCrossentropy` | | Binary `[0, 1, 1]` | `BinaryCrossentropy` | | Continuous numbers | `MeanSquaredError` / `MeanAbsoluteError` | ##### The Functional API `Sequential` only handles a single straight chain. The Functional API handles anything: multiple inputs, multiple outputs, skip connections, shared layers. You call layers on tensors and wire up a graph: ```python from tensorflow.keras import layers, Model image_in = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28), name="image") meta_in = keras.Input(shape=(4,), name="metadata") # e.g. brand, price band x = layers.Flatten()(image_in) x = layers.Dense(256, activation="relu")(x) x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x) m = layers.Dense(16, activation="relu")(meta_in) merged = layers.Concatenate()([x, m]) merged = layers.Dense(128, activation="relu")(merged) category_out = layers.Dense(10, name="category")(merged) price_out = layers.Dense(1, name="price")(merged) model = Model(inputs=[image_in, meta_in], outputs=[category_out, price_out], name="multi_task") model.compile( optimizer="adam", loss={"category": keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), "price": keras.losses.MeanSquaredError()}, loss_weights={"category": 1.0, "price": 0.2}, metrics={"category": ["accuracy"], "price": ["mae"]}, ) ``` A **residual (skip) connection** — the idea behind ResNet and every transformer — is trivial here: ```python def residual_block(x, units): shortcut = x y = layers.Dense(units, activation="relu")(x) y = layers.Dense(units)(y) y = layers.Add()([shortcut, y]) # the skip connection return layers.Activation("relu")(y) ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Input image"] --> B["Flatten → Dense 256"] C["Input metadata"] --> D["Dense 16"] B --> E["Concatenate"] D --> E E --> F["Dense 128"] F --> G["Dense 10
category"] F --> H["Dense 1
price"] ``` Use `Sequential` for simple stacks and the Functional API for everything else. There is also model subclassing (`class MyModel(keras.Model)`), which looks almost exactly like PyTorch's `nn.Module` — useful when you need genuinely custom behaviour. ##### Layers and activations The layers you will use constantly: ```python layers.Dense(units, activation="relu") # fully connected layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding="same", activation="relu") layers.MaxPooling2D(2) layers.Flatten() layers.Dropout(0.3) layers.BatchNormalization() layers.LayerNormalization() layers.Embedding(vocab_size, 128) # for text layers.LSTM(128, return_sequences=True) layers.MultiHeadAttention(num_heads=8, key_dim=64) layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D() ``` Activations can be passed as a string (`activation="relu"`) or as a separate layer (`layers.Activation("relu")`). The separate-layer form is required when you need something between the linear operation and the activation, such as batch normalisation: ```python layers.Dense(128, use_bias=False), # bias is redundant before BatchNorm layers.BatchNormalization(), layers.Activation("relu"), ``` That ordering — Dense → BatchNorm → Activation — is the conventional one and generally trains better than putting BatchNorm after the activation. ##### Callbacks Callbacks are how you inject behaviour into `fit()`. They are the answer to "but I need control" — and they cover most of what you would hand-write in a PyTorch loop. ```python callbacks = [ keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping( monitor="val_loss", patience=5, restore_best_weights=True, # ← crucial; without it you keep the LAST model verbose=1, ), keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint( "artifacts/best_model.keras", monitor="val_accuracy", save_best_only=True, verbose=1, ), keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau( monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=3, min_lr=1e-6, verbose=1, ), keras.callbacks.CSVLogger("artifacts/training_log.csv"), keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir="logs/fit", histogram_freq=1), ] history = model.fit( x_train, y_train, epochs=60, batch_size=64, validation_split=0.1, callbacks=callbacks, verbose=2, ) ``` **`restore_best_weights=True` is the argument people forget.** Without it, `EarlyStopping` halts training but leaves you holding the weights from the *last* epoch — the overfitted ones — rather than the best. It quietly undoes the entire point of early stopping. `ReduceLROnPlateau` is Keras's practical answer to learning rate scheduling: when validation loss stops improving, halve the learning rate. It often buys another point or two of accuracy for free. Plotting the history: ```python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5)) for ax, key in zip(axes, ["loss", "accuracy"]): ax.plot(history.history[key], label=f"train {key}") ax.plot(history.history[f"val_{key}"], label=f"val {key}") ax.set_xlabel("Epoch"); ax.set_ylabel(key); ax.legend(frameon=False) ax.set_title(f"{key.capitalize()} — watch where val turns", loc="left") fig.tight_layout() ``` Writing custom callbacks is straightforward when you need something unusual: ```python class CostAwareStop(keras.callbacks.Callback): def __init__(self, target_acc=0.93): super().__init__() self.target = target_acc def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None): if logs.get("val_accuracy", 0) >= self.target: print(f"\nHit {self.target:.0%} at epoch {epoch}; stopping to save GPU cost.") self.model.stop_training = True ``` ##### Evaluating and saving ```python test_loss, test_acc, test_top3 = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0) print(f"test accuracy {test_acc:.4f} top-3 {test_top3:.4f}") import numpy as np logits = model.predict(x_test[:8], verbose=0) probs = tf.nn.softmax(logits).numpy() # apply softmax manually for logits print(np.array(class_names)[probs.argmax(1)]) # Saving — the modern .keras format holds architecture + weights + optimizer state model.save("artifacts/fashion_model.keras") reloaded = keras.models.load_model("artifacts/fashion_model.keras") # Weights only model.save_weights("artifacts/fashion.weights.h5") # SavedModel format for TensorFlow Serving deployment model.export("artifacts/fashion_savedmodel") ``` The `.keras` format is a single self-contained file — noticeably more convenient than PyTorch, where you must keep the model class definition around to reload a `state_dict`. ##### Common mistakes - **`softmax` on the output layer *and* `from_logits=True`.** Pick one. - **`CategoricalCrossentropy` with integer labels** (use the `Sparse` version) or vice versa. - **`EarlyStopping` without `restore_best_weights=True`.** - **Forgetting to scale pixel values** to [0, 1] or standardise inputs. - **Using `validation_split` on unshuffled, ordered data** — it takes the *last* fraction, so if your data is sorted by class the validation set is one class. - **Confusing `Sequential` limits with model limits**; reach for the Functional API when you need branches. - **Not calling `model.summary()`**, then discovering a shape mismatch three epochs in. - **`BatchNormalization` after the activation** rather than between the linear layer and the activation. - **Ignoring `history`** and never plotting the curves. - **Mixing `tf.keras` and standalone `keras` imports** in the same project. - **Assuming Keras is only for beginners.** It trains production models at Google scale; the API is simple, not the framework. ##### Hands-on: build it twice Your practical task is a Fashion-MNIST classifier with the Sequential API. Time yourself. From a blank file to a trained model with plotted curves should take under fifteen minutes — and noticing that speed is part of the lesson. Then run `model.summary()` and reconcile the parameter count by hand: a `Dense(256)` after flattening 28×28 has 784 × 256 + 256 = 200,960 parameters. Confirming that arithmetic makes the layers concrete. The mini project builds the same model in both Keras and PyTorch and compares the developer experience. Write both, then count lines and note where each was easier. Be specific rather than vague — "Keras handled the validation split, metric tracking, and checkpointing in three arguments; PyTorch needed about 35 lines, but when I wanted to log per-class accuracy mid-epoch, PyTorch was a two-line change and Keras needed a custom callback." That kind of concrete comparison is a genuinely good interview answer to "which framework do you prefer?" The assignment focuses on callbacks: use early stopping and checkpointing, and document how they change training. Run the same model twice — once with 60 epochs and no callbacks, once with early stopping at patience 5. Compare final test accuracy, wall-clock time, and where the validation curve turned. Typically early stopping ends around epoch 20 with equal or better test accuracy and a third of the training time. That is a real, measurable result you can report. ##### Key takeaways - **Keras trades control for speed**: `Sequential` + `compile` + `fit` gets a standard model trained in a fraction of the code a manual PyTorch loop needs. - **Use `Sequential` for straight stacks and the Functional API for branches**, multiple inputs/outputs, and skip connections. - **Return raw logits with `from_logits=True`** — applying softmax twice is the most common Keras bug, and it fails quietly. - **Callbacks are how you regain control**: early stopping (with `restore_best_weights=True`), checkpointing, LR reduction, and logging cover most needs. - **Learn both frameworks.** PyTorch dominates GenAI and research; Keras is faster for standard models and common in production — and the concepts underneath are identical.
